headline: Government Announces $50 Weekly Fuel Relief as MPs Clash Over Diesel Security
summary: The Government announced a temporary $50-a-week boost for eligible working families as fuel prices rise amid the Middle East conflict, while opposition MPs questioned both who qualifies and whether New Zealand is prepared for a prolonged supply disruption. Parliament also debated the Government’s international response to the conflict, advanced bills on policing, tax and Auckland transport, and agreed to progress legislation ending commercial greyhound racing from August 2026.

topicSummaries.topic: $50-a-Week Relief Targets 143,000 Families Amid Fuel-Security Dispute
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The payment could help eligible families with children manage rising fuel and household costs, but people outside the eligibility rules will not receive this specific increase.
topicSummaries.content: Finance Minister Nicola Willis announced a $50-a-week increase to the in-work tax credit from 1 April, expected to reach 143,000 working families with dependent children in full and make a further 14,000 families eligible for a reduced payment. The increase will last until 31 March 2027 or until 91-octane petrol stays below $3 a litre for four consecutive weeks, whichever comes first; the estimated cost is $373 million if it runs for a full year. The Government said it was prioritising targeted help over broader subsidies, while Green and Te Pāti Māori MPs challenged the exclusion of many beneficiaries, students and other households. The announcement came amid a separate dispute over fuel preparedness: the Opposition questioned the cancellation of a proposed 70-million-litre diesel reserve and the Government’s emergency escalation triggers; ministers pointed to higher minimum stockholding requirements and reported 50 days of petrol, 45 of diesel and 44 of jet fuel.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chlöe Swarbrick (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Will the Prime Minister remove his new obligations and financial sanctions on nearly half a million beneficiaries—that is, over 40,000 more since he took office—in this fossil fuel crisis, or will he extend support as announced today to those beneficiaries so that they can afford to get to job interviews?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Beneficiaries are receiving, as of 1 April, a cost of living adjustment, reflecting, essentially, the cost of living, but the low and middle income working New Zealanders who wake up each and every day, who drive to work, who take their kids to school, and who are working incredibly hard are the ones who are hurt the most through this period.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Defends Strait of Hormuz Statement as Opposition Warns of Military Risks
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: New Zealand’s stance on the conflict could affect its international relationships, the safety of its personnel and the costs of fuel and trade at home.
topicSummaries.content: An urgent debate examined New Zealand’s participation in a joint statement condemning Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and expressing readiness to contribute to efforts to ensure safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Labour’s Vanushi Walters and other opposition speakers argued the wording could create expectations of military involvement and questioned whether the Government had fully assessed legal, security and financial risks. Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters said the statement supported freedom of navigation, not a definite military deployment, and that any possible contribution would be a Cabinet decision. Government and opposition MPs also clashed over whether New Zealand had adequately condemned US and Israeli attacks on Iran. The debate ended without a vote on the Government’s position.

keyExchanges.speaker: Vanushi Walters (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The Government has now placed New Zealanders in a lose-lose situation.

keyExchanges.speaker: Winston Peters (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: That is not the same as saying we are definitely going to contribute.

topicSummaries.topic: Greyhound Racing Closure Bill Passes Second Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed ban would end commercial greyhound racing in New Zealand while setting up a process to rehome dogs and support people whose work and livelihoods depend on the industry.
topicSummaries.content: The House agreed to the second reading of the Racing Industry (Closure of Greyhound Racing Industry) Amendment Bill, which provides for commercial racing to end on 1 August 2026 and establishes a transition agency to oversee the wind-down. Racing Minister Winston Peters cited 16 race-related fatalities and 822 injuries, including 250 serious injuries, in the 2024-25 season. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori supported the bill, while speakers stressed the need for humane rehoming and practical support for affected workers and families. The select committee amendments allow TAB NZ to continue taking bets on overseas greyhound races to help fund the transition, require a later review of that arrangement, and direct residual transition-agency assets to former industry participants. ACT supported the second reading but said its support at the final stage would depend on credible compensation plans.

keyExchanges.speaker: Winston Peters (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: In the most recent 2024-25 racing season, there were 16 race-related greyhound fatalities, equating to 0.47 fatalities per 1,000 racing starts. There were also 822 race-related injuries, of which 250 were serious injuries.

keyExchanges.speaker: Cameron Luxton (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: ACT is voting in favour of the second reading of this bill, but we cannot continue to support it at third reading unless we see credible compensation plans from the Minister.

topicSummaries.topic: Police Information-Gathering Bill Advances Despite Privacy and Profiling Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill could broaden police authority to record images and sounds and close public areas, raising questions about privacy, oversight and the treatment of Māori and young people.
topicSummaries.content: The Policing Amendment Bill passed its first reading by 102 votes to 21 and was referred to the Justice Committee, with a report due by 27 July 2026. Police Minister Mark Mitchell said it would clarify police powers to collect images, sounds and other information for lawful purposes, including intelligence, and expand temporary closure powers to a wider range of accessible areas. He said limits and oversight would prevent mass surveillance. Labour MPs sought details on data storage, retention, safeguards and consultation; Green and Te Pāti Māori MPs cited previous findings about police photographing members of the public, including Māori young people, and warned the bill could entrench unfair practices. ACT supported referral to select committee but made its continued support conditional on stronger privacy protections and accountability.

keyExchanges.speaker: Mark Mitchell (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I want to be very clear that this bill will not provide additional powers to Police that could be construed as enabling mechanisms for mass surveillance of the New Zealand public.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tamatha Paul (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: What this bill is enabling is widespread surveillance, and the impact will disproportionately hit Māori, because half of those photos that the police had on their devices were Māori.

topicSummaries.topic: Tax Bill Advances as Parties Dispute Privacy and Wealth Transparency
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill changes tax rules for workers, investors and businesses, while its information-sharing provisions affect how taxpayer and trust information may be collected and used.
topicSummaries.content: The Taxation (Annual Rates for 2025–26, Compliance Simplification, and Remedial Measures) Bill passed its second reading by 68 votes to 55. The Government said the changes would simplify compliance, adjust rules for digital nomads and foreign investment funds, and exempt qualifying income from selling excess household electricity to the grid. Labour and the Greens opposed provisions removing Inland Revenue’s specific power to collect information for tax-policy research and changing trust disclosures; Labour also raised concerns about wider sharing of tax information between government agencies and the privacy safeguards around it. National, ACT and New Zealand First supported the bill, arguing that it would reduce barriers for visitors, returning New Zealanders and businesses. Further debate and consideration of amendments remain ahead.

keyExchanges.speaker: Deborah Russell (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: At this stage, the Labour Party continues to oppose this bill, and the reason is around the sharing of information.

keyExchanges.speaker: David Wilson (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: This is a pragmatic piece of legislation that fixes technical glitches while clearing the path for Kiwis to come home—we quite like that.

topicSummaries.topic: Government-Backed Loans to More Than Double Public EV Chargers
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: More public charging points could make electric vehicles a more practical option for drivers, including as fuel costs and supply concerns rise.
topicSummaries.content: Transport Minister Chris Bishop said $52.7 million in zero-interest loans from ChargeNet and Meridian would support enough public electric-vehicle chargers to lift the national total from more than 1,800 to about 4,500. The chargers are planned for major centres and regional areas, contributing towards the Government’s target of 10,000 by 2030. Bishop said loans would bring forward private investment and offer better value for taxpayers than grants. Green MP Tamatha Paul challenged the Government’s view that drivers do not need taxpayer subsidies to adopt electric vehicles.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Kiwis are already making the shift to electric vehicles, and they don’t need taxpayer subsidies in order to do so

topicSummaries.topic: Auckland Transport Governance Bill Returns Decisions to Elected Representatives
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to who controls Auckland’s roads and public transport could influence local transport choices, planning and accountability for services residents use every day.
topicSummaries.content: The House began the second-reading debate on legislation to transfer most Auckland transport planning and local-road functions from Auckland Transport to Auckland Council and local boards, while refocusing Auckland Transport as a public-transport delivery body. The bill also establishes a joint central-government and council regional transport committee to prepare a 30-year plan. The Government cited low public confidence in Auckland Transport, while Labour and the Greens supported greater local accountability and also raised concerns about funding and the role of central government. Te Pāti Māori said the bill should go further in guaranteeing Māori representation and embedding Te Tiriti obligations. ACT backed the shift but criticised aspects of existing cycling, parking and traffic measures. The debate was interrupted at adjournment and is due to resume; the House had not yet voted on the second reading.

keyExchanges.speaker: Julie Anne Genter (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: I think the changes in this bill will bring about better democratic accountability to the people of Auckland for transportation decisions, and I think that will be a good thing.

keyExchanges.speaker: Simon Court (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: If you don’t like Auckland Council approving stupid speed humps everywhere, we’ll be able to vote them out

conclusion: The Government advanced targeted household relief and several major bills, but debates over who receives support, how public powers are safeguarded and how New Zealand should respond to the Iran conflict remained unresolved.
